---
title: "Sampling and the discrete Fourier transform"
description: "What happens to a signal when you only measure it at discrete points: the Nyquist frequency, aliasing, leakage, and rebuilding a signal from a few frequencies."
toc: true
execute:
  enabled: false
---

Every recording is a list of numbers taken at discrete times, and the Fourier
transform is how we ask such a list which frequencies it contains. The
transform itself is a one-line formula. What takes getting used to is the way
sampling changes what the formula can tell you: measure too slowly and a fast
oscillation shows up as a slow one, record for too short a time and a clean
peak smears out. This page lets you produce those effects on purpose, with a
signal whose true content you know.

Everything runs in your browser, and the figure updates as soon as you move a
slider.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// shared helpers: one persistent canvas per explorable, text-sized fonts, responsive width
exFont = ({size: getComputedStyle(document.body).fontSize, family: getComputedStyle(document.body).fontFamily, toString() { return this.size + " " + this.family; }})
exFg = () => getComputedStyle(document.body).color
mkCanvas = (W, H) => {
  const c = DOM.context2d(W, H);
  c.canvas.style.width = "100%"; c.canvas.style.maxWidth = W + "px"; c.canvas.style.height = "auto";
  return c;
}
axisBox = (c, x, y, w, h) => { c.strokeStyle = "#999"; c.lineWidth = 1; c.strokeRect(x, y, w, h); }
```

## The setup

The signal is the sum of two sine waves,

$$y(x) = a_1 \sin(2\pi f_1 x) + a_2 \sin(2\pi f_2 x),$$

with frequencies $f_1$ and $f_2$ in cycles per unit length and amplitudes
$a_1$ and $a_2$. I write the variable as $x$ rather than $t$ because the same
mathematics applies to a signal in space, for instance a pattern of activity
along a strip of cortex, but you can read it as time throughout.

We do not get to see $y(x)$ itself. We see $N$ samples $y_n = y(x_n)$ taken
at points spaced $\Delta x$ apart over an interval of length $T$, so that
$N = T / \Delta x$. The discrete Fourier transform (DFT) of these samples is

$$Y_m = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} y_n\, e^{-2\pi i\, m n / N},$$

and it tells us how much of each frequency $f_m = m / T$ is present. Two
facts about these frequencies are the whole point of the page.

First, the frequencies are spaced $1/T$ apart. A longer recording gives a
finer frequency grid. If a true frequency of the signal does not fall on the
grid, the DFT has to represent it with a mix of neighbouring grid
frequencies, and the peak spreads out. This is called leakage.

Second, the grid stops at the Nyquist frequency $f_{\text{Ny}} = 1 / (2
\Delta x)$, half the sampling rate (Nyquist 1928; Shannon 1949). A sine wave needs at least two samples per
cycle to be told apart from a slower one. If the signal contains a frequency
above $f_{\text{Ny}}$, the samples are indistinguishable from the samples of
a lower frequency, and the DFT reports that lower frequency instead. This is
aliasing, and once it has happened there is no way to undo it from the
samples alone. The same effect makes wagon wheels appear to turn backwards in
films.

The last slider, $K$, uses the transform in the other direction. It keeps the
$K$ strongest frequencies in the spectrum, throws the rest away and rebuilds
the signal from what is left. If the spectrum is clean, two components are
enough to reproduce the signal exactly. If it is not, you need more.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof ftF1 = Inputs.range([0, 12], {value: 1, step: 0.1, label: "f₁ (cycles / unit)"})
viewof ftA1 = Inputs.range([0, 2], {value: 1, step: 0.1, label: "a₁"})
viewof ftF2 = Inputs.range([0, 12], {value: 3.5, step: 0.1, label: "f₂ (cycles / unit)"})
viewof ftA2 = Inputs.range([0, 2], {value: 0.5, step: 0.1, label: "a₂"})
viewof ftDx = Inputs.range([0.02, 0.5], {value: 0.1, step: 0.01, label: "Sampling interval Δx"})
viewof ftT = Inputs.range([1, 8], {value: 4, step: 0.5, label: "Interval length T"})
viewof ftK = Inputs.range([0, 10], {value: 2, step: 1, label: "K components kept for reconstruction"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
ft = {
  const T = ftT, dx = ftDx, N = Math.max(4, Math.floor(T / dx)), x0 = -T / 2;
  const sig = x => ftA1 * Math.sin(2 * Math.PI * ftF1 * x) + ftA2 * Math.sin(2 * Math.PI * ftF2 * x);
  const xs = Array.from({length: N}, (_, n) => x0 + n * dx), ys = xs.map(sig);
  const M = Math.floor(N / 2), re = new Float64Array(M + 1), im = new Float64Array(M + 1);
  for (let m = 0; m <= M; m++) for (let n = 0; n < N; n++) { const a = -2 * Math.PI * m * n / N; re[m] += ys[n] * Math.cos(a); im[m] += ys[n] * Math.sin(a); }
  const amp = Array.from({length: M + 1}, (_, m) => ({m, f: m / T, A: (m === 0 ? 1 : 2) * Math.hypot(re[m], im[m]) / N, ph: Math.atan2(im[m], re[m])}));
  const kept = amp.slice(1).sort((a, b) => b.A - a.A).slice(0, ftK);
  const rec = x => amp[0].A * Math.cos(amp[0].ph) + kept.reduce((s, c) => s + c.A * Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * c.f * (x - x0) + c.ph), 0);
  const fine = Array.from({length: 600}, (_, i) => x0 + T * i / 599);
  const fNy = 1 / (2 * dx);
  const alias = f => { const fs = 2 * fNy; let g = Math.abs(f - Math.round(f / fs) * fs); return g; };
  return {T, dx, N, x0, xs, ys, fine, sig, rec, amp, kept, fNy, alias};
}
ftCanvas = mkCanvas(760, 450)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const c = ftCanvas, fg = exFg(), W = 760, H = 450, blue = "#1f77b4", orange = "#ff7f0e";
  const {T, N, x0, xs, ys, fine, sig, rec, amp, kept, fNy, alias} = ft;
  c.clearRect(0, 0, W, H); c.font = exFont;
  // signal panel
  const sP = {x0: 80, y0: 12, w: W - 100, h: 170};
  const ymax = Math.max(0.5, ftA1 + ftA2) * 1.15;
  const sx = x => sP.x0 + sP.w * (x - x0) / T, sy = y => sP.y0 + sP.h * (1 - (y + ymax) / (2 * ymax));
  axisBox(c, sP.x0, sP.y0, sP.w, sP.h);
  c.strokeStyle = "#888"; c.lineWidth = 1; c.beginPath(); c.moveTo(sP.x0, sy(0)); c.lineTo(sP.x0 + sP.w, sy(0)); c.stroke();
  c.strokeStyle = "#aaa"; c.lineWidth = 1.5; c.beginPath(); fine.forEach((x, i) => i ? c.lineTo(sx(x), sy(sig(x))) : c.moveTo(sx(x), sy(sig(x)))); c.stroke();
  c.strokeStyle = orange; c.lineWidth = 2; c.beginPath(); fine.forEach((x, i) => i ? c.lineTo(sx(x), sy(rec(x))) : c.moveTo(sx(x), sy(rec(x)))); c.stroke();
  c.fillStyle = blue; xs.forEach((x, n) => { c.beginPath(); c.arc(sx(x), sy(ys[n]), 3.5, 0, 2 * Math.PI); c.fill(); });
  c.fillStyle = fg; c.textAlign = "center"; c.fillText(`x  ·  N = ${N} samples`, sP.x0 + sP.w / 2, sP.y0 + sP.h + 22);
  c.textAlign = "right"; c.fillText("y", sP.x0 - 10, sP.y0 + sP.h / 2 + 5);
  c.fillText(ymax.toFixed(1), sP.x0 - 8, sP.y0 + 6); c.fillText((-ymax).toFixed(1), sP.x0 - 8, sP.y0 + sP.h + 2);
  // spectrum panel
  const pP = {x0: 80, y0: 240, w: W - 100, h: 140};
  const fmax = Math.max(fNy * 1.05, 0.5), Amax = Math.max(0.5, ...amp.slice(1).map(a => a.A)) * 1.15;
  const fx = f => pP.x0 + pP.w * f / fmax, fy = A => pP.y0 + pP.h * (1 - A / Amax);
  axisBox(c, pP.x0, pP.y0, pP.w, pP.h);
  c.setLineDash([4, 4]); c.strokeStyle = "red"; c.beginPath(); c.moveTo(fx(fNy), pP.y0); c.lineTo(fx(fNy), pP.y0 + pP.h); c.stroke();
  c.strokeStyle = "#2ca02c";
  for (const [f, a] of [[ftF1, ftA1], [ftF2, ftA2]]) if (a > 0) { const g = alias(f); c.beginPath(); c.moveTo(fx(g), pP.y0); c.lineTo(fx(g), pP.y0 + pP.h); c.stroke(); }
  c.setLineDash([]);
  for (const a of amp.slice(1)) {
    const isKept = kept.includes(a);
    c.strokeStyle = isKept ? orange : blue; c.lineWidth = isKept ? 3 : 1.5;
    c.beginPath(); c.moveTo(fx(a.f), fy(0)); c.lineTo(fx(a.f), fy(a.A)); c.stroke();
    c.fillStyle = isKept ? orange : blue; c.beginPath(); c.arc(fx(a.f), fy(a.A), 3, 0, 2 * Math.PI); c.fill();
  }
  c.fillStyle = fg; c.textAlign = "center";
  c.fillText(`frequency (cycles / unit)  ·  Nyquist ${fNy.toFixed(2)}`, pP.x0 + pP.w / 2, pP.y0 + pP.h + 22);
  c.fillText("0", fx(0), pP.y0 + pP.h + 42); c.fillText(fmax.toFixed(1), fx(fmax), pP.y0 + pP.h + 42);
  c.textAlign = "right"; c.fillText("|Y|·2/N", pP.x0 - 10, pP.y0 + pP.h / 2 + 5);
  c.fillText(Amax.toFixed(1), pP.x0 - 8, pP.y0 + 6); c.fillText("0", pP.x0 - 8, pP.y0 + pP.h + 2);
  return c.canvas;
}
```

## Reading the figure

The upper panel shows the signal. The thin grey curve is the true continuous
$y(x)$, which in a real experiment you would never get to see. The blue dots
are the samples, the only thing the transform has access to. The orange curve
is the signal rebuilt from the $K$ strongest frequencies. When the orange
curve lies on top of the grey one, the reconstruction has recovered the
signal from its samples.

The lower panel is the amplitude spectrum. There is one stem for each grid
frequency $f_m = m/T$, with the height scaled so that a pure sine of
amplitude $a$ gives a stem of height $a$. The red dashed line marks the
Nyquist frequency, where the grid ends. The two green dashed lines mark where
the true frequencies $f_1$ and $f_2$ ought to appear. If a true frequency lies
above Nyquist, its green line is drawn at the frequency it gets aliased to,
so you can see the stem land in the wrong place. Stems used in the
reconstruction are drawn in orange, the rest in blue.

With the default settings everything is well behaved. Both frequencies sit
on the grid, both are below Nyquist, the spectrum shows two clean stems of
heights $a_1$ and $a_2$, and with $K = 2$ the reconstruction is perfect.

## Things to try

Raise $f_2$ slowly past the Nyquist frequency, which is 5 cycles per unit at
the default sampling interval. Just below it the stem still sits where it
should. Just above it, the green line and the stem jump to a lower
frequency, and the orange reconstruction now contains a slow oscillation that
was never in the signal. Look at the blue dots in the upper panel while you
do this: they genuinely are consistent with that slower wave. Then make the
sampling interval smaller. Nyquist moves up, the fast component is resolved
again, and the problem goes away. That is the one reliable cure for aliasing:
sample faster, or filter out the fast components before you sample.

Set $f_1$ to 1 and change $T$ from 4 to 4.5. The signal has not changed, but
the grid has, and 1 cycle per unit no longer lies on it. The single stem
turns into a cluster around the true frequency. With $K = 2$ the
reconstruction is now visibly wrong, and you need to raise $K$ to get the
signal back. The general lesson is that the width of a peak in a spectrum is
set by the recording length, not by the signal, and that a sharp peak needs a
recording that is long compared to the period.

Set both amplitudes to the same value and bring $f_1$ and $f_2$ close
together. At some point the two stems merge into one, and no setting of $K$
separates them. The frequency resolution is $1/T$, so two frequencies closer
than that cannot be distinguished, no matter how finely you sample.

This page is based on the Fourier exercises in Dayan and Abbott (2001). The
transform here is computed by the direct sum, which is fine for a few hundred
samples. For anything larger one uses the fast Fourier transform of Cooley
and Tukey (1965), which gives the same numbers in a fraction of the time.
Press et al. (2007) is a practical reference for both the algorithm and the
pitfalls of sampling.

## References

complex Fourier series. *Mathematics of Computation* 19: 297–301.

Dayan P, Abbott LF (2001). *Theoretical Neuroscience: Computational and

*Transactions of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers* 47: 617–644.
